newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Ministerial slip.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Ministerial slip.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
Remember the week before the election when John Howard said he'd be giving his ministers a free rein?
They would take full responsibility for running their portfolios.
They would stand or fall by dint of their own efforts and there would be plenty of competition from keen young backbenchers to provide the prod, he said.
Fast forward to the last two weeks.
Howard's inexperienced ministers are beginning to fray, particularly under pressure.
It's worth remembering that only Howard himself and Industry Minister John Moore have tasted ministerial duty before -- in Malcolm Fraser's team.
But it seems some of the lessons of the Fraser days have been forgotten.
One of the hallmarks of that government was the dominance of the prime minister, his office and his ever-expanding department.
Ministers constantly complained (out of the prime minister's earshot) of being second guessed by his advisers, officials or the big man himself.
Before the latest election that seemed to be a feature Howard was determined not to repeat.
But it wasn't long before the prime minister was spreading himself across the portfolios.
The most visible example is in health, where the responsible minister, Michael Wooldridge, chose to be overseas in the crucial post-budget period.

The revelation that a raft of health insurance funds had either received approval for premium rises, or were about to seek them, was a major blow to one of the central planks of the government's health changes, designed to reactivate the private sector.
First Howard chose to leave the mess to the acting minister, Jocelyn Newman.
Then he decided to get involved by writing himself into the approval process.
It wasn't long before his advisers realised this was a mistake.
Any future rise would no longer be sheeted home to some arcane bureaucratic process, but to the prime minister himself.
That's putting your field marshal in the very front line.
The solution -- as it is so often in government -- was an inquiry.
Howard's team let a little pressure build up with everyone from the biggest health funds, through the various hospital associations to the Opposition calling for a public inquiry.
And that's what they got -- an inquiry into the health insurance industry.
This too is dangerous territory.
As has been observed often in politics, never set up an inquiry without a pre-determined outcome and tight parameters.
Howard's tried to satisfy the latter by ruling out any discussion of Medicare's role, an attempt to make an omelette without breaking eggs.
As the government will discover, even this hobbled inquiry is bound to traverse some dangerous ground.
It will become implicit, at the least, that the coalition's policy to offer tax breaks for private health insurance is simply bad, band-aid policy.
It's economic effect could be none other than to increase costs in the private sector of the industry without solving the fundamental problem of adequate funding for the public system.
And it's been the prime minister's initiative.
He won't be able to slough this one off to Wooldridge.
He wasn't even in the country when the succession of panic moves were made.
But more broadly what this indicates is the way Howard will operate in the future.
Any political bushfire, regardless of size, is likely to have the prime minster on the hose, with all the risks that carries.
But it's clear that Howard may need also to remind his front-line troops of the consequences of relaxing their discipline.
Communications Minister Richard Alston at the outset was seen by government advisers as potentially one of the more accident-prone ministers.
They were encouraged by his early performances but he was obviously too enamoured by his own success and last Sunday let his guard down.

In one swoop he rocked the delicately-poised Senate position on the Telstra bill with the loose line that full privatisation was both inevitable and desirable; upset the Fairfax group by musing on a possible break-up; and put down the new ABC chairman, Donald McDonald (his own appointment) by declaring the national broadcaster's cuts would be made, whatever the chairman thought.
Howard didn't hide his anger, publicly rebuking Alston.
Effectively he's on notice, joining Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer.
It's understood Howard's office has also demanded all junior ministers clear their news releases with the prime ministerial team before despatch.
All of which will put growing pressure on the prime minsiter's office and on the man himself, particularly when there's real trouble on several fronts.
(Views are those of the author, not those of Reuters)
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
